source: Dhami, Belton, de Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation, Study 1 layout effect
finding: Three layouts of the same 2-hypothesis, 12-evidence task. Only hypotheses in rows with evidence in columns cut confirm-only choices. The ACH layout (hypotheses in columns) and a paragraph per hypothesis did not.
numbers: N=161 between subjects (HypCol n=55, HypRow n=51, HypText n=55). Task 1 confirm-only (CONS) choice: HypCol 61.8% (34/55), HypRow 39.2% (20/51), HypText 67.3% (37/55). chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009, phi=.24. Bonferroni post hoc: HypRow p=.003; HypCol p=.327; HypText p=.048 borderline.
quote: individuals presented with hypotheses in rows and evidence items in columns were significantly less likely to demonstrate confirmation bias
limits: Not preregistered. UK university students, mean age 20, 90.1% female. Only 2 hypotheses and 12 items. Paper and pencil, no time limit. Post hoc tests compare each layout to 50/50, not layouts to each other. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Layout changed strategy with identical information. If real, it is a design choice for how S4 shows hypotheses against evidence. One weak study: test in our own loop.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) Study 1 credibility sensitivity
finding: Layout did not change whether people switched their choice when the evidence for A was discredited (Tasks 3A to 3B).
numbers: Of those who chose A in 3A, switched to B in 3B: HypCol 77%, HypRow 78%, HypText 75%. chi2(2)=0.15, p=.927, phi=.04. Excluded for choosing B in 3A: 18% HypCol, 15% HypRow, 35% HypText.
limits: Exclusion is unequal across layouts (35% dropped in text). Sensitivity is a binary switch, not a graded weight.
agent_relevance: The layout effect is about one-sided versus balanced use, not about weighting by source quality. Credibility weighting needs its own mechanism, not a layout.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) validity of the strategy label
finding: The choice-based strategy label matched coded self-report and usefulness ratings, so the layout effect is not just noise in the label.
numbers: Task 1 choice vs coded self-report chi2(2)=28.85, p<.001, phi=.49; 74.6% of A-choosers said they relied only on consistent evidence. Usefulness of C/CC M=5.64 vs I/II M=5.05, t(90)=2.43, d=0.26. 35 open answers not codable, 2 missing.
limits: Usefulness effect is small (d=0.26). One task per person gives the label in Study 1.
agent_relevance: A task with a known diagnostic answer measures strategy cheaply. We can build the same probe for an LLM.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) rival explanations offered for the row advantage
finding: Authors offer three untested reasons: sequential per-hypothesis processing uses less working memory; the horizontal visual field and eye movements dominate; reading runs left to right. The ACH layout forces item-by-item scanning across hypotheses.
numbers: No mechanism manipulated. Recall of the layout did not differ: HypCol 76.4%, HypRow 74.5%, HypText 60.0%, chi2(2)=4.19, p=.123.
limits: Speculation. The vision argument fits Western readers only; no cross-cultural test. Text grouped by hypothesis also failed to help, which weakens a plain grouping account.
agent_relevance: No eye-movement story for an LLM. Testable variables: grouping axis (per hypothesis vs per evidence) and what is adjacent in token order.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) Study 2, Dutch military analysts in the ACH layout
finding: 62 Dutch analysts and cadets, all given the ACH layout, mostly did not show confirmation bias. Most balanced consistent and inconsistent evidence.
numbers: N=62 (80% male, mean age 32.5). CONS 19.4%, INCONS 14.5%, BAL 66.1%. Credibility-sensitive overall 83.3%: BAL 98%, CONS 72.7%, INCONS 33.3%. CRT M=2.32 vs students 0.51, d=2.05.
limits: No layout comparison in Study 2, so it cannot test the layout effect. Volunteers at training start. Not preregistered. Different populations compared across studies.
agent_relevance: Experts weigh both sides even in the worse layout. Layout may matter most for weaker reasoners; a strong model may be less layout sensitive (see b19, b20).

source: Dhami et al. (2024) individual differences
finding: Cognitive reflection predicted strategy in students but not in analysts. Judgment coherence (additivity) predicted nothing.
numbers: Study 1: CRT M=0.27 (A choosers) vs 0.81 (B choosers), t(116)=3.88, p<.001, Glass d=0.54. Study 2: CONS 2.25 vs others 2.34, t(60)=0.30, p=.763, d=0.10. Additivity vs strategy d=0.04 (S1), d=0.13 (S2). 91.9% of analysts nonadditive, 67.7% subadditive.
limits: CRT floor effect in students (mean 0.51 of 3). Mostly female students; CRT runs lower in women.
agent_relevance: No reliable individual-difference moderator. Do not use a coherence score as a quality proxy in agent logic.

source: Dhami, Belton, Mandel (2019) The analysis of competing hypotheses in intelligence analysis, Applied Cognitive Psychology 33(6):1080-1090
finding: RCT with 50 UK analysts: ACH-trained analysts did not follow all steps; evidence of bias reduction was mixed; ACH may have raised inconsistency and error. Abstract page only.
numbers: N=50, half trained. The abstract has no figures. The 2024 paper (opened) reports 80% of the untrained group redrew the data as an ACH-style matrix on their own, and ACH analysts were less internally consistent.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; the full-text PDF download failed. Other figures come from the 2024 summary.
agent_relevance: People choose the matrix spontaneously, yet the matrix layout did not reduce bias in Study 1. Spontaneous choice is not evidence the layout is good.

source: Maegherman, Ask, Horselenberg, van Koppen (2020) ACH in a legal setting, as summarised in Dhami et al. 2024
finding: RCT with law students: ACH training did not beat a bias-information control on evidence search or likelihood ratings. About a third used the matrix.
numbers: N=191. Both groups chose more disconfirming than confirming questions and rated exonerating evidence more important. About 1/3 of the ACH group used the matrix; rated helpfulness 57/100.
limits: Second-hand, read only through the Dhami 2024 text. Legal task, not intelligence.
agent_relevance: An independent null for the matrix as an intervention. Low uptake means a matrix the agent must fill adds load that people avoided.

source: Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy, as summarised in Dhami et al. 2024
finding: Post-task data from the 50-analyst RCT: ACH may reduce logical coherence of probability judgments and raise mean absolute error and rank error.
numbers: Summary only; no figures. See folder 01 for numbers.
limits: Second-hand; not opened.
agent_relevance: A matrix procedure can make probabilities worse. Presentation by code should show, not force, a scoring rule.

source: Sui, Zhou, Zhou, Han, Zhang (2024) Table Meets LLM, WSDM
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on a 7-task table-structure benchmark. Serialization format changes accuracy; HTML was best; putting the question after the table cost accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 downstream: TabFact NL+Sep 70.26, Markdown 68.40, JSON 68.04, XML 70.00, HTML 71.33; HybridQA HTML 47.29 vs JSON 42.40; ToTTo BLEU HTML 12.30 vs Markdown 8.57. GPT-4 with HTML: TabFact 78.40, HybridQA 56.68, SQA 75.35, Feverous 83.21. Best benchmark config 65.43% overall. Question after table: -6.81% overall. Zero-shot vs 1-shot: -30.38% with HTML. Format explanation hurt cell lookup.
limits: 2023 GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only. Downstream gains are a few points, larger on structure tasks. Single run per cell.
agent_relevance: Format matters; HTML or delimiter text beat Markdown here. Put task and context before the table. Include one worked example.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Rethinking Tabular Data Understanding with LLMs, perturbation results
finding: On WikiTableQuestions with GPT-3.5, transposing a table or shuffling its rows lowers accuracy. Python-agent reasoning is far more fragile than text reasoning.
numbers: 837 questions x 4 variants. Direct prompting: original 59.50, row-shuffled 52.21 (-12.25%), transposed 51.14 (-14.05%), both 37.51 (-36.96%). Python agent: 55.91, 47.91 (-14.31%), 12.45 (-77.73%), 8.96 (-83.97%). PDF table text was garbled; mapping reconstructed from the percent drops. LLM as transposer 53.68% and 51.07%. [cross-check: labels were swapped]
limits: GPT-3.5 only, one dataset, zero-shot. Column shuffling skipped because earlier work found little effect.
agent_relevance: Orientation changes LLM accuracy by 12% or more and the model cannot reliably fix it. Code should normalise orientation, not ask the model to transpose.

source: Liu et al. (2023) NORM table structure normalisation
finding: A two-stage normaliser (detect column tables, transpose to row tables, then sort rows) recovered most of the loss.
numbers: With NORM, direct-prompt accuracy 58.66 across all perturbations (original 59.50); Python agent with NORM 52.45. Content-aware heading choice: 97.39% (first row) and 94.77% (first column).
limits: GPT-3.5 only. The content-aware step still relies on the LLM spotting headings.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S4 presentation by code: canonicalise layout in code before the model sees it, so layout noise is removed rather than tuned.

source: Deng et al. (2024) Tables as Texts or Images (arXiv 2402.12424v5)
finding: Five text and three image table representations over six benchmarks with GPT-4, Gemini Pro and Llama-2. The best representation depends on model and dataset. Brackets marking row boundaries help weaker models. Row colours slightly help GPT-4 on images.
numbers: GPT-4 average 63.8%, GPT-3.5 55.2%, Llama-2-70B 50.0%. Expert prompting beat vanilla by 3.5% and CoT by 1.2% for GPT-4 on text tables. Image CoT: column colour 58.0 vs vanilla 57.8 (GPT-4), 45.1 vs 46.0 (Gemini). On WikiTQ and TabFact text beat image significantly; on FinQA the image helped GPT-4.
limits: Gains mostly under 4 points. Brackets can hurt strong models. Wikipedia tables are likely in pretraining as text, which favours text.
agent_relevance: Explicit row delimiters help weak models and may hurt strong ones. The best S4 layout may depend on the model.

source: He et al. (2024) Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?
finding: The same content in plain text, Markdown, YAML and JSON changes GPT accuracy a lot. Larger models are more consistent but not immune.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo varies up to 40% on code translation. Markdown to plain text: +200% on FIND (GPT-3.5); JSON to plain: +300% on HumanEval (GPT-4-32k). MMLU example: JSON +42% vs Markdown. Consistency GPT-3.5 below 0.5, only 16% identical answers Markdown vs JSON; GPT-4 above 0.5. Best-vs-worst matched t-test mostly p<0.01.
limits: Relative changes, sometimes from very low baselines. OpenAI GPT models only.
agent_relevance: No universal best format. Validate any layout on the target model with several formats and report the range.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design, ICLR
finding: Meaning-preserving formatting changes (separators, casing, spacing) shift few-shot accuracy by up to 76 points for LLaMA-2-13B. Size, more examples and instruction tuning do not remove it. Format performance correlates only weakly across models.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points (LLaMA-2-13B); about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks and several models. Proposes FormatSpread to report a performance interval.
limits: Open-source models, few-shot classification tasks; effects are likely smaller on current strong chat models.
agent_relevance: A layout comparison with one template is not trustworthy. Any S4 layout test must sample many formats and report the spread.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang, Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Order of premises changes accuracy though the logic is unchanged. Forward order (same as the proof) is best for every model. Weaker models suffer more.
numbers: Logic: shuffling costs GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L up to 20-30%; Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5 fall from over 65% to under 25%. R-GSM reorder: GPT-4-turbo 94.1 to 85.0, PaLM 2-L 86.4 to 79.5, Gemini Pro 80.5 to 69.1, GPT-3.5 67.3 to 51.8. A second set: 100% to 89.9, 87.9, 74.6, 64.9.
limits: Synthetic deduction with distractors; R-GSM is a constructed set. The drop grows with the number of rules.
agent_relevance: For evidence lists, order by dependency or by hypothesis in code. Match presentation order to reasoning order.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Models do best when the relevant item is first or last in the context and worst in the middle (U-shaped curve).
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA drops by more than 20% when the answer moves to the middle. At 20 and 30 documents the worst case falls below closed-book accuracy (56.1%).
limits: Older models; newer long-context models may reduce the effect (not tested here).
agent_relevance: In a long evidence matrix the middle rows get less attention. Cap matrix size or give per-hypothesis slices.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors, ICLR
finding: 20 LLMs prefer certain option IDs (A, B, ...), so answers change when the same options are reordered. The bias is mostly a token prior on the ID and can be reduced at inference by estimating the prior with permutations (PriDe).
numbers: 20 LLMs, three benchmarks. Bias measured as the standard deviation of per-option recall (RStd).
limits: Multiple choice only. Exact accuracy gains not recorded this session.
agent_relevance: If S4 labels hypotheses, the label and position bias the pick. Permute labels in code and aggregate by content.

source: Cross-study pattern: layout effects shrink with model strength (Chen 2024; He 2024)
finding: In the LLM layout studies read here, stronger models lose less than weaker ones, but none are immune.
numbers: Premise order on R-GSM: GPT-4-turbo drops 9.1 points, GPT-3.5 drops 15.5. Format consistency: GPT-4 above 0.5, GPT-3.5 below 0.5.
limits: Synthesis by this agent from opened papers; models are 2023 vintage.
agent_relevance: Expect 2026 models to be less layout sensitive. Test current models before building S4 layout rules.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) design critique of cell-by-cell scoring
finding: The authors argue that the ACH layout, which asks for item-by-item scoring of each cell, discourages thinking about dependencies between evidence items and burdens memory for tracking consistent and inconsistent cells per hypothesis.
numbers: No numbers. Backed by the 2019 finding that only a minority added up consistent evidence alone and most added both.
limits: Argument, not a test.
agent_relevance: A cell scored one at a time hides correlated evidence (G4). Code should compute tallies, while the model checks dependence separately.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) limits stated by the authors
finding: More work is needed: vary the number of hypotheses and evidence items, separate balanced from inconsistent-only strategy, test collaborative use.
numbers: Study 1 could not separate BAL from INCONS (one task). Tasks fixed at 2 hypotheses, 12 items. Data at osf.io/hcdp3.
limits: Authors' own admission.
agent_relevance: The boundary conditions of the layout effect are unknown. Test at 3 to 7 hypotheses, the real ACH range.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) literature claim that the matrix helps
finding: The belief that the ACH-style matrix improves analysis (Heuer 2005; Davies and Gustafson 2017) had no direct test of the layout before Study 1.
numbers: Authors: no research had examined an ACH-style matrix with hypotheses in columns. Prior tests (Lehner 2008, Kretz 2012 and others) used small samples.
limits: The authors' statement about the literature as of 2024.
agent_relevance: The popular layout is untested folklore. Do not copy it into S4 on authority.

source: Information-display classics (Payne 1976; Bettman and Zins; Jarvenpaa 1989; Schkade and Kleinmuntz 1994), not opened
finding: From memory: in decision research, how a matrix is organised (by alternative or by attribute) steers processing order, and people tend to process along the organised dimension.
numbers: No figures recorded. Not opened; OpenAlex and arXiv rate limits blocked abstract retrieval.
limits: Memory only. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Supports the grouping-axis mechanism, matching Dhami 2024. Read before use.

source: Gap: no LLM test of hypotheses-in-rows vs hypotheses-in-columns found
finding: No study found that tests hypotheses-in-rows against hypotheses-in-columns on an LLM. Targeted searches could not run: the web search budget was exhausted and arXiv and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429.
numbers: Zero direct studies found; the table-format studies above are indirect.
limits: Absence of evidence under tool limits, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: A gap for our own experiment: same evidence in three layouts (hypothesis rows, evidence rows, prose); measure confirm-only picks and credibility switches.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) portable task design and human baselines
finding: The task ports easily to an LLM: Task 1 uses counts so confirm-only tallying picks A while balanced or disconfirm-only picks B. Tasks 3A/3B discredit the evidence for A and test whether the choice flips.
numbers: 2 hypotheses, 12 evidence items, classes C, CC, I, II, NA. Human baselines: students 56.5% confirm-only, analysts 19.4%; credibility switch 75-78% students, 83.3% analysts.
limits: Appendix item text not extracted here; materials on OSF.
agent_relevance: Gives human baselines to compare an LLM against under each layout.

source: Dhami et al. (2024) mechanism candidates for the layout effect
finding: Three rival accounts: working-memory load from simultaneous tracking, processing order set by the grouping axis, and visual or reading conventions. Study 1 cannot tell them apart.
numbers: Text grouped by hypothesis did not help (67.3% confirm-only), which fits the grouping-axis account only if prose adds its own load.
limits: Inference by this agent from the opened paper; no discriminating experiment exists.
agent_relevance: For LLMs, reading convention is irrelevant and working memory becomes attention limits (b17, b19). Test grouping directly by randomising which axis is grouped.
